title: Design a Movie Ticket Booking System
summary: BookMyShow in an hour. The class diagram is routine; the interview is decided entirely by one question — what stops two people buying seat H12 at the same instant, and what happens to the hold when one of them wanders off.

blocks.title: What you are actually being asked
blocks.text: Every candidate produces `Movie`, `Theatre`, `Screen`, `Show`, `Seat`, `Booking`. That diagram earns you nothing — it is assumed. The entire signal is in **seat contention**: how you stop a double-booking, how long you hold a seat, and what happens when the holder closes the tab.
The problem

A city has theatres; theatres have screens; screens run shows of a movie at a time; each show has seats. A user searches for a movie, picks a show, selects seats, pays, and receives a booking. Two users must never end up with the same seat.
Clarify before you code

items.title: Can a user hold seats before paying?
items.text: Yes — every real system does, and this is the question. A hold with a TTL is the answer; how you expire it is the follow-up.

items.title: How long is the hold?
items.text: Five to ten minutes in practice. It has to be long enough for payment and short enough that a walk-away does not strand inventory.

items.title: Seat pricing — flat, or by class?
items.text: Recliner, premium, standard. Another strategy interface, and worth a sentence, not five minutes.

items.title: Partial booking allowed?
items.text: If a user asks for five seats and only three are free — all or nothing, or best effort? All-or-nothing is almost always right and simpler to reason about.

items.title: Cancellations and refunds?
items.text: Confirm scope. A cancellation returns a seat to the pool, which reopens every concurrency question you just answered.

blocks.text: Class design

blocks.title: Routine, and worth ten minutes at most
blocks.caption: `ShowSeat` is the one that matters: seat availability is a property of the **show**, not of the physical seat. Modelling availability on `Seat` is the mistake that makes the whole thing unworkable.
blocks.code:
classDiagram
    class Show {
        -String id
        -Movie movie
        -Screen screen
        -Instant startsAt
        -Map~String, ShowSeat~ seats
    }
    class ShowSeat {
        -Seat seat
        -SeatStatus status
        -String heldBy
        -Instant holdExpiresAt
        -Money price
    }
    class Seat {
        -String label
        -SeatClass seatClass
    }
    class Booking {
        -String id
        -User user
        -Show show
        -List~ShowSeat~ seats
        -BookingStatus status
        -Money total
    }
    class BookingService {
        +Hold hold(String showId, List~String~ seats, User u)
        +Booking confirm(String holdId, Payment p)
        +void release(String holdId)
    }
    Show o-- ShowSeat
    ShowSeat --> Seat
    Booking o-- ShowSeat
    BookingService ..> Show

blocks.title: Availability belongs to the show, not the seat
blocks.text: Seat H12 is a piece of furniture used by ten shows a day. If `Seat` carries a `booked` flag, booking the 6pm show marks it taken for the 9pm one too. `ShowSeat` — the seat *within a show* — is the unit of inventory, and getting that right in the first two minutes signals you have thought about this before.
The seat lifecycle

blocks.title: Three states and a clock
blocks.caption: `HELD` is the state that exists purely because payment takes time. Everything hard about this problem lives in getting out of it.
blocks.code:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Available
    Available --> Held : hold() succeeds
    Held --> Booked : payment confirmed
    Held --> Available : user cancels
    Held --> Available : hold expires (TTL)
    Booked --> Available : booking cancelled
    Booked --> [*] : show starts

blocks.text: Stopping the double-booking
Two users, one seat, same millisecond. Read-then-write loses:

blocks.caption: Four ways to fix it, in ascending order of realism.
rows: Correct in one process. Dies the moment there are two app servers
`UPDATE show_seats SET status=HELD WHERE id=? AND status=AVAILABLE`
The database does the atomicity. Zero extra infrastructure — **the answer to give**
`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` over the requested seats
Correct, but holds a transaction open across user think-time if you are careless
Works across services; now you own lock expiry and the fencing-token problem

blocks.title: Two details that separate answers
blocks.text: The `OR (status = 'HELD' AND hold_expires_at < now())` clause makes expiry **lazy** — an expired hold is reclaimed by the next person who wants the seat, with no sweeper required. And rolling back a partial claim is what enforces all-or-nothing. Volunteering both is the strongest thing you can do in this question.
Expiring holds

blocks.caption: Do both. Say why.
rows: A seat can look taken on the seat map long after the hold died
Runs at an interval, so it is always slightly behind
Your inventory now lives in two places that can disagree

blocks.title: Lazy for correctness, sweeper for the UI
blocks.text: Lazy reclaim guarantees nobody is ever *blocked* by a dead hold. The sweeper exists so the seat map does not lie to people browsing. They solve different problems and that is why real systems run both.
Payment, and the failure that matters
Confirmation is two systems agreeing: the payment provider and your seat inventory.

items: **Charge, then confirm** — a crash between the two takes money without a seat. Recoverable by a reconciliation job; the customer is furious in the meantime.
**Confirm, then charge** — a failed payment leaves a booked seat nobody paid for. Worse: it is silent.

**The real answer:** the hold *is* the reservation. Charge while holding, and confirm only on a successful charge. If the charge fails, the hold expires on its own and the seat returns. **A payment webhook must be idempotent on the hold id**, because providers retry.

blocks.title: Idempotency is not optional
blocks.text: Payment providers deliver the same webhook more than once. `confirm(holdId)` must be safe to call twice — the second call returns the existing booking rather than creating a second one. A booking table with a unique constraint on `hold_id` makes this true by construction.
Complexity

rows: Search shows by movie and city
O(log n) with an index on (city, movie, startsAt)
O(seats in show) — a few hundred
O(1) — one status change plus an idempotent booking insert

blocks.text: Follow-ups you should have ready

items.title: Two app servers
items.text: The `synchronized` answer dies; the conditional update does not. That is the reason to give it first rather than reaching for a distributed lock.

items.title: Prevent single-seat gaps
items.text: Cinemas dislike leaving one orphaned seat mid-row. This is an allocation policy over contiguous runs — a nice strategy-interface follow-up.

items.title: Dynamic pricing
items.text: `PriceStrategy` per show: weekend, opening night, seat class, occupancy-based surge. The price must be captured **on the hold**, or it can change under the user mid-payment.

items.title: Handle a flash sale
items.text: Ten thousand people, one popular show. A queue in front of the booking service, and optimistic concurrency behind it. This is the HLD pivot.

items.title: Cancellations and refunds
items.text: Return seats to the pool, and decide whether a refund window exists. Note that returning a seat re-opens every race you just closed.

items.title: Show a live seat map
items.text: Push updates over websockets, and accept that the map is eventually consistent — the conditional update remains the only source of truth.

blocks.text: Edge cases to state before you are asked

items: Two users requesting overlapping seat sets — the conditional update grants one and rolls back the other entirely.
A user holding seats who never returns → the hold expires and the seats come back without anyone intervening.
Payment succeeding *after* the hold expired → refund, or re-attempt the claim. Never confirm a booking on seats you no longer hold.
A show starting while seats are held → holds are void once the show begins.
Booking zero seats, or more than the per-user maximum → rejected at validation.
A duplicate payment webhook → idempotent on the hold id, returns the existing booking.

blocks.text: What you are graded on

rows: Conditional update; the check *is* the write
A TTL hold as an explicit state
Lazy reclaim for correctness, sweeper for the UI
An answer that survives a second app server

blocks.title: The 45-minute plan
blocks.text: **0–5** clarify holds, TTL, partial booking. **5–15** classes — fast, and make sure `ShowSeat` lands. **15–22** the seat lifecycle. **22–34** the double-booking problem and the conditional update; this is the graded part, so do not rush it. **34–40** hold expiry, lazy plus sweeper. **40–45** payment idempotency.
